Twenty-three comments

Sir John Fenwick’s The Flower Amang Them A’

This is a well-known air in Northumbrian music circles, a moderately-paced listening piece. I don’t know whether its origins are in NE England or elsewhere; nor do I know who Sir John Fenwick was, though the name’s Northumbrian. It was recorded in the early years of the folk revival by The High Level Ranters and also Horslips; Kathryn Tickell and no doubt others have recorded it since. It’s a natural on the harp, and wouldn’t be out of place among Carolan’s tunes (there are one or two other Northumbrian airs that could just as easily have been Irish, by the sound of them).

Sir John Fenwick was a Northumbrian Jacobite nobleman who lived for some of his life at Wallington Hall. Born around 1645, he was executed in 1697 for plotting against King William III.

Guitarist Paul Newman adds another anecdote about the history of the tune when he introduces it.

There were apparently words to go with this tune and people were executed for singing the song.

Re: Sir John Fenwick’s The Flower Amang Them A’

Surprised its not been mentioned before but O‘Carolan tune No 179 (often also called Planxty Scott), bears a striking similarity to Sir John Fenwick etc. In 6/8 not 3/4 but the two are often interchangeable. So the 1st posting is correct about the O’Carolan link. I have recordings of it by Andi Wolfe ‘An Obair’, Broceliande ‘Sir Christemas’ and Tabby Finch ‘Cloud Cover’ under the 179 title. Such an eaarworm of a tune, its easy to see how it moved around and changed titles in whichever direction.

Mary Scott, Flower Of Jarrow, X:4

This is a very simple version of this tune and I believe closer to the way I learnt it from the High Level Ranters a long while ago. I prefer to play it singly, but you can of course make the first 16 bars into an A part and repeat it, same with the B part.
I have rather cheekily renamed it, giving its original name. I read somewhere that the disreputable politician, John Fenwick used this Border tune as a rally call for his supporters at election. Whereas the tune is named after the wife of a notorious reiver a hundred years earlier, Walter Scott of Harden.
In D to suit flute players.

Sir John Fenwick from Bewick’s Pipe Tunes

A verbatim copy of Sir John Fenwick from Bewick’s Pipe Tune. This was compiled by Robert Bewick, son of the Northumbrian wood engraver, Thomas Bewick. Although, Bewick was one of the first people to play keyed smallpipes, which extended their range, this tune was from an earlier period where the chanter had only an octave range. He acquired keyed pipes around 1800.

The tune is written in G, the standard key for the instrument. Northumbrian pipers read the music in G whilst actually playing it in F.

↳ Posted by Jim Sime on September 7th, 2025.

Sir John Fenwick in D (from Bewick’s Pipe Tunes)

Just a transposition to D of the Robert Bewick version. Penny whistle players can often only read music in D. So if they want to play in G, they need the D version. It exactly like Northumbrian pipers reading the music in G but playing it in F on their F chanters. Or, indeed, highland pipers reading in A and playing in B flat. It’s a mixed up world of sugar curls…

↳ Posted by Jim Sime on September 7th, 2025.

Re: Mary Scott, Flower Of Yarrow :5

@Jim Sine - Nice to see Bewick’s setting here. I’ve been playing this tune for as long as I’ve been piping and always struggled with the high A in the second part (high B for me, I play it in A) until Matt Seattle (who compiled the Bewick collection for publication) pointed out that this and other early settings are single octave tunes. I’ll maybe transcribe my setting later.

Incidentally, G is a perfectly normal key for whistle players who can read the dots, it fits perfectly on a D tin whistle. Fair enough for tunes in Bb or something to transpose to D for whistle players, but no need for G.
